Moeurn subsequently appealed his sentence, asserting that the trial court had erred in calculating his offender score insofar as it had included a washed out juvenile conviction for attempted assault as part of his criminal history. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Moeurn's sentence, holding that Washington Revised Code §9.94A.525(4) requires that anticipatory offenses be treated as completed offenses for purposes of classifying prior convictions, thereby extending the wash out period for Moeurn's conviction for attempted assault from the five years applied to Class C felonies to the ten years applied to Class B felonies. Thus, as Moeurn had not spent ten years in the community without committing a crime subsequent to his conviction for attempted assault, the conviction had not washed out. Moeurn appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.94A.525(4) extend the wash out period for anticipatory offenses?
conclusions: Justice Alexander's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that language in §9.94A.525(4) requiring that anticipatory offenses be treated as completed offenses does not extend the wash out period for anticipatory offenses but rather simply requires that anticipatory offenses that have not yet washed out be treated as completed offenses in calculating an offender score. Thus, the Court vacated Moeurn's sentence and remanded the case for resentencing.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Curtis v. Lein
facts: Petitioner Tambra Curtis filed suit against respondent Jack Lein in the Superior Court for King County after she was injured when a dock located on property owned by Lein collapsed beneath her. As Lein had removed the dock prior to trial and it therefore could not be examined to determine the cause of the collapse, Curtis attempted to invoke the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur, asserting that although she could not demonstrate that the dock had collapsed due to negligent maintenance, a reasonable inference of negligence on Lein's part could be drawn as a dock would not ordinarily collapse unless its owner had negligently maintained it. The trial court granted summary judgment to Lein and dismissed the case, ruling that res ipsa loquitur could not be invoked as a number of causes other than negligent maintenance could have been responsible for the collapse. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's decision. Curtis appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur be invoked in premises liability cases in which the burden of proof is on the plaintiff to demonstrate that the respondent knew or should have known about a dangerous situation on their property?
conclusions: Justice Stephens' opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case, holding that although explanations for the collapse other than a discoverable defect existed, Curtis could nonetheless invoke the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur as the accident was of a type that would not ordinarily occur in the absence of negligence, the dock was under Lein's exclusive control, and it was uncontested that Curtis did not contribute in any way to the accident. Thus, Curtis could rely upon res ipsa loquitur to shift the burden of proof to Lein to demonstrate that the faulty condition of the dock was not due to a discoverable defect.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Seattle Times Company v. Serko
facts: The petitioner Seattle Times Company requested public records related to the fatal shootings of four police officers from the Pierce County Sheriff's Office pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56). The alleged accomplices of the shooter subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County to enjoin the release of the documents, asserting that the records were not subject to disclosure under §42.56 as their release would impair their right to a fair trial. Respondent Judge Susan Serko's decision for the court agreed, ruling that the alleged accomplices' right to a fair trial would be impaired by the records' release. In response, the Seattle Times Company petitioned the Supreme Court of Washington for a writ of mandamus compelling Serko to order the requesed records' release.
questions: Did Judge Serko's order enjoining the release of the requested documents properly apply §42.56?
conclusions: Justice Stephens' opinion for a unanimous Court granted the writ of mandamus, concluding that Serko's order had been improper insofar as the exception to §42.56's disclosure requirements for investigative records does not apply to records related to investigations that have resulted in charges being brought and are therefore no longer ongoing. The Court also held that any order withholding public records on grounds that their release would jeopardize a defendant's right to a fair trial must be based upon a specific finding that unfairness and/or prejudice will result and must consider alternatives. As Serko's order was not and had not done so, the Court vacated the order.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Washington v. Marohl
facts: After forcing Joseph Peterson to the floor during an altercation, causing Peterson to suffer minor injuries, petitioner James Marohl was convicted of second degree assault in the Superior Court for Mason County. Marohl subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the floor of the casino in which the altercation occurred was not an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm for purposes of establishing second degree assault under Washington Revised Code §9A.36.031(1)(d). The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Marohl's conviction. Marohl appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Marohl commit second degree assault by using the floor as an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm?
conclusions: Justice Sanders opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and held that insufficient evidence existed to convict Marohl of second degree assault insofar as the floor could not be an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm given that under the circumstances of the case it was not likely to produce harm and was not used as a weapon.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Washington v. Wilson
facts: After reaching a plea agreement with prosecutors, petitioner Jason Wilson pled guilty to two counts of identity theft in the Superior Court for Grays Harbor County and was sentenced. When it was subsequently revealed that Wilson's offender score had been improperly calculated insofar as a previous conviction for a gross misdemeanor had been counted as a felony conviction and that Wilson's sentence was therefore erroneous, Wilson moved to be resentenced. The trial court denied Wilson's motion, ruling that Wilson's only remedy was to withdraw his guilty plea. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals concluded that Wilson's offender score had in fact been correctly calculated and affirmed Wilson's sentence on grounds that Washington Revised Code §9.94A.525(4) requires anticipatory offenses to be scored the same as if they were convictions for completed offenses in calculating offender scores. Wilson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.94A.525(4) require anticipatory offenses to be scored the same as if they were convictions for completed offenses in calculating offender scores? If not, is Wilson entitled to be resentenced?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that §9.94A.525(4) only requires an anticipatory offense to be scored the same as if it were a conviction for a completed offense in calculating an offender score when the anticipatory offense is itself a felony. As Wilson's offender score had therefore been improperly calculated, the Court also concluded that the trial court's error had been an error of law rather than an error of fact and that Wilson was therefore entitled to be resentenced despite his consent to the plea agreement.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Washington v. Coucil
facts: Petitioner Nikeemia Coucil was charged with felony harassment in the Superior Court for King County and released on bail pending trial. After Coucil subsequently failed to appear for a pretrial hearing, he was also charged with bail jumping. Following his apprehension, Coucil was ultimately convicted of the lesser crime of misdemeanor harassment and, in a separate trial, of bail jumping. At sentencing, the trial court classified the bail jumping conviction as a felony on grounds that Coucil was being charged with a felony at the time he failed to appear. Coucil appealed his sentence, asserting that the bail jumping conviction should have been classified as a misdemeanor given that, despite initially being charged with felony, he was ultimately convicted of a misdemeanor. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Coucil's sentence, holding that Washington Revised Code §9A.76.170 classifies bail jumping for sentencing purposes according to nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear rather than according to the nature of the underlying charge's ultimate disposition. Coucil appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the penalty imposed for bail jumping pursuant to §9A.76.170 contingent upon the nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear or upon the nature of the underlying charge's ultimate disposition?
conclusions: Justice Alexander's opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §9A.76.170 unambiguously bases the penalty for bail jumping upon the nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear as to hold otherwise would prevent bail jumping charges from being litigated until underlying charges were litigated.
